Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Inter for text and Space Grotesk for headings are good defaults when nothing in the request or the subject calls for other type. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside the `:root` padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets the `:root` padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

The second model now includes the temperature rules, the designer uses them, and the new website is live: [Temperature-Aware Primer Designer](https://claude.ai/artifact/JRi6KEZtGsBqdkP5jUspZ7). It's private until you share it. All tests pass, and the Python and both websites give identical designs on all 80 comparison cases.

**A note on the biology for the write-up:** the DNA unwinds at the 95 °C step, not at annealing. The annealing temperature matters in two other ways:
- **Primers must stay bound at it.** If a primer's Tm is too close to the annealing temperature, part of the template goes uncopied each cycle. That was the problem with our old designs.
- **A higher annealing temperature is more specific,** because only well-matched sites hold at it.

**Second model (now version 2).** It checks four temperature rules. I set each limit from the CDC assays, which are known to work:

| Rule | Limit | CDC assays |
|---|---|---|
| Primer Tm above the annealing temperature | 6–13 °C above | every primer is at least 6.6 °C above 55 °C |
| Difference between the two primers | at most 4 °C | N1 is 3.7 °C |
| Probe Tm above the higher primer | at least 2 °C | 2.6–6.3 °C |
| Product Tm | at most 90 °C, so it melts apart at the 95 °C step | |

Each oligo's Tm now uses the CDC's real amounts: 500 nM per primer and 125 nM probe. There are 4 new test cases. The CDC N1, N2, N3 and RNase P assays all pass, and our old N gene designs fail, each for the reason found earlier.

**Designer (now version 4):**
- **Lengths:** chosen to aim primers at annealing + 8 °C (63 °C) and the probe at + 15 °C (70 °C), then ranked by how close each oligo is to its target.
- **N gene result:** the new designs have primers at 62.8–63.1 °C and probes at about 70 °C. At Primer-BLAST's conditions they fall inside its 57–63 °C range, so Primer-BLAST would now accept them too.
- **GC-only mode:** the old behaviour is still available with `annealing_c=None`, so the 15 earlier designer tests and the first website are unchanged. There are 5 new temperature tests.

**New website, in `website_temperature/`:**
- **Inputs:** an annealing temperature box and a "Use melting temperature" switch, so you can compare against GC alone.
- **Results:** each oligo's Tm, the product's Tm, and a thermometer scale on every design showing where each Tm sits.
- **Explanations:** sections on the two-step cycle and the rules.
- The old site in `website/` is unchanged.

**Things to know:**
- **Low-GC targets now often get no design.** Test case 2 (30.5 % GC) can't reach 61 °C with primers of at most 24 bases. The page says why.
- **The test-case file describes only the GC-only site.** The expected results in `test_cases_web_specificity.txt` don't match the new site; its own expected results still need writing.
- **Still not modelled:** hairpins and primer dimers, and Tm for sites with an insertion/deletion or two mismatches side by side.

None of this is committed yet. It will be when you say bye.

content.text:
Yes, that's the reason. A primer that melts too close to the annealing temperature only partly stays bound, so the designer only accepts primers with a Tm at least 6 °C above it. The designer never simulates binding failing; it just enforces that rule. Our primers also have to stay 18–24 bases and 40–60 % GC, so their Tm can only go so high. The higher you set the annealing temperature, the fewer stretches of the gene can reach the required Tm.

Here's what that does on the N gene:

| Annealing | Primer Tm needed | Positions that can reach it (of 1,066) | Possible designs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 °C | ≥ 56 °C | 1,065 | 45,746 |
| 55 °C | ≥ 61 °C | 1,023 | 53,212 |
| 60 °C | ≥ 66 °C | 701 | 22,756 |
| 65 °C | ≥ 71 °C | 118 | 260 |
| 68 °C | ≥ 74 °C | 4 | 0 |

The real-world reason behind the rule: at a high annealing temperature, a primer that's too short or too AT-rich would spend much of each cycle floating free, and the PCR would copy less template each round. In a real lab you'd fix that with longer or more GC-rich primers. Our designer's limits (at most 24 bases, at most 60 % GC) don't allow that, so above about 65 °C it runs out of options. The N gene is also fairly AT-rich (SARS-CoV-2 is about 38 % GC), which makes this happen sooner.

Two other effects add to it:
- **The probe has the same problem:** its Tm must be 2 °C above the higher primer, so it also has to reach a higher Tm.
- **Low temperatures cut designs too:** 50 °C gives fewer designs than 55 °C. Primers are also capped at annealing + 13 °C, so at 50 °C any primer above 63 °C is rejected. A primer that binds far more strongly than needed also holds on to sites with mismatches, which makes it less specific.

So there's a best range for each target: high enough for specificity, low enough that the gene's sequence can still reach the Tms. For this gene that's roughly 55 °C, which matches the CDC's protocol. If you want, I can add a sentence like this to the website so the drop in designs at high temperatures is explained on the page.

content.text:
The model now does everything in that paragraph, and the website shows it: [Temperature-Aware Primer Designer](https://claude.ai/artifact/JRi6KEZtGsBqdkP5jUspZ7), now updated. All tests pass, and the Python and both websites still agree on all 86 comparison cases.

**Your paragraph, point by point:**

| The proposal says | Status |
|---|---|
| Tm from the nearest-neighbour stacking model (SantaLucia 1998) | already done; matches Primer3 and Primer-BLAST |
| Margin against the annealing temperature | already done |
| Salt and primer concentration set by the user | **new**: five settings on the website (K⁺/Na⁺, Mg²⁺, dNTPs, primer amount, probe amount) |
| Mismatches by count and position, not as a stability penalty | **the model differs** (below) |
| Primer dimers: align at every offset, sum the paired region's energies | **new** |

**Mismatches: decide which description you want.** The second model already goes further than the proposal says. It uses published mismatch parameters (Allawi & SantaLucia) to compute how much a mismatch lowers the Tm, which the first model's count-and-position report can't. So you can either update the proposal or report to describe that, or keep the proposal's simpler framing and mention the Tm calculation as an extension.

**Primer dimers:**
- **Method:** every pair of oligos, and each oligo with itself, is lined up at every offset, and the stacking energy of each paired region is summed. A region can span single mismatches, using the parameters the model already has.
- **Limits:** a design is skipped if any dimer is more stable than −9 kcal/mol at 37 °C. If the dimer pairs a primer's 3′ end, which the polymerase can extend, the limit is −5. The probe's 3′ end doesn't count, because TaqMan probes are blocked there.
- **The CDC assays pass easily.** Their most stable dimer is −5.9, and their most stable 3′-end dimer is −3.1.
- **Checks:** one value worked out by hand matches exactly, and a primer pair built to dimerise is caught.
- **For your write-up:** these values come out 1–4 kcal/mol weaker than Primer3's. Primer3 also counts bases dangling past the paired region, and loops. That's why I set the limits using the CDC assays with this same method.
- **On the website:** each design shows its most stable dimer as an alignment, and the summary says how many designs were skipped for dimers.

**Two things worth knowing:**
- **The new N gene design 1 has a fairly strong dimer.** Its reverse primer and probe share a CAG-repeat stretch, giving a 10 bp dimer at −8.1 kcal/mol. That passes the −9 limit and isn't at a primer's 3′ end, but it's more stable than any CDC dimer.
- **Still not modelled:** hairpins, where an oligo folds back on itself. That needs loop parameters. The page says so.

**Speed:** the dimer check made the slowest test case take 10.5 seconds on the website. It now takes 2.1, with identical results. The N gene takes about 3 seconds.

Version 1 is unchanged, and none of this is committed yet. It will be when you say bye.

## Log 13 · 2026-11-13 · The website, and product length as a range

**Commit:** `4b95102`

### What I did
- Built the first website: paste a genome and a target gene, pick the
  mismatch allowance and product length, and get primers and a probe back,
  best match first. Each design shows a small map of where the forward
  primer, probe and reverse primer sit in the product **(#59)**.
- A browser can't run Python, so the designer (and the parts of the first
  model it uses) was translated into JavaScript. To make sure the
  translation is right, `check_website_port.py` runs the Python and the
  JavaScript on the same inputs: all 35 checks give exactly the same
  primers, positions and warnings **(#59)**.
- I couldn't copy long sequences out of the terminal, so the website got
  buttons that load each test case and run it. I also wrote
  `test_cases_web_specificity.txt`: 5 cases that cover good, low, high-but-ok
  and too-high GC, and a second copy of the target that matches perfectly,
  with 2 mismatches or fewer, or with more than 2 **(#60)**.
- Testing the website, I saw the product length should be a range, not one
  number. Now it's a shortest and a longest (default 60-150 bp), designs
  stay inside it, and shorter products rank higher because they amplify
  best in qPCR. With this, the N gene's best design (28275-28334) sits right
  next to the CDC N1 assay (28287-28358) **(#61)**.

### Things to work on for next time
- **Compare with NCBI:** BLAST our designed primers (and the CDC ones)
  against NCBI's databases to see where else they match (other viruses, the
  human genome), and compare that with our first model's one-site check.
  Also run NCBI Primer-BLAST on the N gene with the same settings and
  compare its primers with ours.
- **Main goal:** finish the second model (Tm and the annealing temperature):
  Tm for indel and side-by-side mismatch sites (#44), the CDC's real
  concentrations, and the probe's Ct delay (#45). Then add it to the
  website (Tm and how much of each oligo is bound at 55 C).
- Report where each CDC design ranks among the designer's options (#52).
- Move the CDC published-primer check into `journal/`, and add RNase P once
  the human RPP30 segment is downloaded from NCBI.
- Make `primer_design.py` give a clear error for non-DNA letters, like the
  website does, instead of crashing.

---

## Where things stand
Still open (details at the end of `modification documentation.md`): a few
search limits, one genome per variant, and no real Alpha genome yet (#42).
Factor 2 (annealing temperature) has a first version (Log 9). Next: Tm for
indel sites, the CDC's real concentrations, and turning the probe's weaker
binding into an expected Ct delay.

Primer design (Logs 11-12) works on fake genomes: 18-24-base primers,
40-60% GC, best match first, and a product length the user can choose. The
CDC primers pass its rules but are not reproduced yet. The website (Log 13)
runs the same designer in the browser, checked against the Python. Next:
compare with NCBI BLAST and Primer-BLAST, and finish the second model.

## Log 13 · 2026-11-13 · The website, and product length as a range

**Commit:** `4b95102`

**#59. Problem:** the planned website has to run in a browser, which cannot
run Python.
**Fix:** `website/primer_design.js` translates `primer_design.py` and the
first-model functions it uses (`build_kmer_index`, `find_binding_sites`,
`candidate_starts`, `compare_site`, `find_indel_sites`, `pair_into_products`,
`probe_inside`, `product_status`, ...) function by function; each JS function
names the Python one it copies. Near-miss search and printing are left out.
One addition: `checkLetters` gives an error for non-DNA letters (the Python
raises a `KeyError`). N/ambiguous positions are found once per genome
instead of on every call (same answer, faster). `website/index.html`: genome
box (paste or open a FASTA file), target box, allowance (0-2), product
range; ranked design cards with an SVG map of the product, the reverse
primer shown 3'->5' with its order sequence, and copy buttons.
`website/example_data.js`: NC_045512.2 and its N gene for the example.
Published as a private artifact (https://claude.ai/artifact/XKd9SSGhpFHH1WXYemP3Bh).
`journal/check_website_port.py` runs both versions on the same inputs (via
macOS `osascript -l JavaScript`, so no Node) and compares designs,
positions, penalties, counts and warnings/errors: 35 of 35 identical.

**#60. Problem:** copying long sequences from the terminal didn't work.
**Fix:** buttons on the page load each test case and run it.
`test_cases_web_specificity.txt`: 5 cases (genome = 100 random + 200-base
target + 100 random, cases 2-4 + 50 random + a second copy):
1. good GC (46.0 %), no copy -> 2 designs
2. low GC (30.5 %), copy with every 6th base changed (3-4 mismatches per
   primer) -> warning, 1 design; the copy never counts
3. high-but-ok GC (66.0 %), every 12th base changed (1-2 mismatches) ->
   warning; a design at allowance 0 and 1, none at 2
4. good GC, exact copy -> no design
5. 89.0 % GC -> error

The same sequences are in `example_data.js` (`TEST_EXAMPLES`), and
`check_website_port.py` runs each at allowance 0, 1 and 2.

**#61. Problem:** the product length was one number with +/- 50 bp around
it; testing the website, a range was more natural.
**Fix:** `design_primers(..., min_product=60, max_product=150)` (CLI: 4th
and 5th arguments). `PRODUCT_RANGE` = (60, 150) replaces `IDEAL_PRODUCT` and
`PRODUCT_SPREAD`; `product_range` was removed. `match_penalty` now adds
(product - min_product) / 10, so shorter products rank higher. Errors:
shortest < 54 bp, longest < shortest, target shorter than the shortest.
Warning when the range goes outside 60-150. Same change in
`primer_design.js` and the page (two boxes). Tests: Case 2 (60 bp -> 0,
150 bp -> 9; the hand example is still 12), Case 14 (70-90 and 250-350),
Case 15 (53-150, 150-60, 59-base target); 15 cases pass.
`test_cases_primer_design.txt` rewritten as version 3. CDC check with the
default range: the designer's first choices are 60 bp products; N1's
(28275-28334) is next to the CDC N1 product (28287-28358).

**Process note (not a model problem):** `save_journal.py` reads stdin, so
inside a combined command it waited forever and swallowed a heredoc commit
message (no commit was made). It is now run as
`python3 .claude/hooks/save_journal.py < /dev/null`.

---

## Still open (known limits after version 4)
- Near-miss and small-gap searches need an exact 6-base stretch (#15, #40).
- Near-miss limits (#16, #17) were tuned on random sequence, not real genomes
  with repeats.
- Severity is a two-level rule (#20); real effects also depend on
  neighbouring bases and positions beyond the 3' window.
- Sites running off the start print negative positions (e.g. -3-48).
- Input is not cleaned of pasted spaces or line breaks.
- The k-mer index is rebuilt on every run; the test suite takes ~10 s.
- The mismatch allowance can only be changed in the code.
- Variants checked with one isolate each (#33).
- No real Alpha (B.1.1.7) genome: the file saved as Alpha was Beta (#42).
- Severity still does not change "binds"; only a HIGH 3' risk changes the
  product status, to "at risk" (#41). Mild mismatches near the 3' end and
  severe ones elsewhere are warnings only.
- Binding at the annealing temperature is an equilibrium estimate (#45), not
  a predicted Ct or efficiency.
- Tm is not computed for indel sites (no bulge-loop parameters) or two
  mismatches side by side (no tandem-mismatch parameters) (#44).
- Tm uses 250 nM for every oligo (the Primer3 reference); CDC uses 500 nM
  primers and 125 nM probe (about 1 C difference).
- Hairpins and primer dimers are not modelled.
- Primer design (#47-#57): ranks only by GC and product length, so many
  designs tie at a perfect 0 and the earliest wins; it does not reproduce
  the CDC designs; never proposes degenerate bases (CDC N3 probe has a Y);
  no hairpin or primer-dimer check; RNase P not checked (needs the human
  RPP30 segment from NCBI).

## Planned (not built yet)
- **Primer design, next:** compare with NCBI BLAST (our primers against
  NCBI's databases) and Primer-BLAST (its designs for the N gene); report
  each published design's rank; move the CDC check into `journal/`; add the
  second model's Tm to the website.
Factor 2's basic plan (nearest-neighbor Tm, Primer3's salt correction,
mismatch parameters, comparison with the 55 C annealing step, fraction
bound) was built in Log 9 (#43-#45). Still to do for it:
- **Indels and tandem mismatches:** add bulge-loop (SantaLucia & Hicks 2004)
  and tandem-mismatch parameters so those sites get a Tm too.
- **CDC concentrations:** 500 nM primers, 125 nM probe, and the master mix's
  real Mg2+ (check the CDC instructions for use).
- **Probe-specific check (TaqMan).** The probe is cleaved only if it is bound
  when the polymerase arrives. CDC probes sit about 10 C above the primers. A
  probe mismatch (e.g. Omicron N1, -6.8 C) can lower the signal and give a
  later Ct without losing the product. Turn fraction bound into an expected
  Ct shift.
- **Primer suggestions on the website:** rank pairs by `STATUS_ORDER_AT_TA`,
  with "at risk" and "weak binding" flagged and suggested last (#41, #45).
- **Later factors:** hairpins and primer-dimers (Primer3 ΔG columns already in
  `primer3_reference_tm.tsv`), the RT step (reverse primer starts the cDNA;
  RNA secondary structure at the site), and the CDC run conditions (primer and
  probe concentrations, cycling).
- **More genomes per variant**, and confirm C28311T across Omicron BA.1
  sequences (#33, #37).
- **Spike-targeting comparison assay.** Hypothesis: oligos in regions under
  strong selection (spike, especially the receptor-binding domain and
  antibody sites) gain mismatches across variants faster than oligos in
  functionally constrained regions (CDC N1/N2/N3 in the N gene). The change
  is driven by selection, not GC content, and shows up over months as
  variants replace one another, not within a few replication cycles.
  Plan: add a spike primer/probe set to `data/primers/` (the Yale spike
  Δ69-70 assay, Vogels et al. 2021, was found in Log 8), run it with both
  models alongside N1/N2/N3, and compare mismatch counts, `three_prime_risk`
  and dTm per variant. Its probe across Alpha's ΔH69/V70 doubles as the
  positive control (should fail on Alpha and Omicron BA.1; needs a real
  Alpha genome, #42).

# 02120 qPCR primers and covid-19
#qPCR
# qPCR primer specificity across SARS-CoV-2 variants

02-120 Programming for Scientists, Fall 2026.

## Scientific question

Do qPCR primer sets designed early in the pandemic still match the genomes of
Alpha, Delta, and Omicron? Which targets keep matching, which acquire
mismatches, and where in the primer do those mismatches fall?

## What the program will do

Given a primer pair and a genome, predict every PCR product the pair would
amplify. A k-mer index locates candidate binding sites on both strands,
mismatches are allowed and scored by distance from the 3' end, and sites
facing each other at a plausible distance are paired into products. A harness
runs published primer sets against each variant genome and reports which
targets survive.

## Checks

- CDC N1, N2, and N3 must each give one product on the reference genome, at
  the amplicon sizes published in Lu et al. (2020).
- Primer sites planted by hand in short synthetic sequences, including
  reverse-strand and single-mismatch cases.
- Nearest-neighbor melting temperatures compared against Primer3 at matched
  salt and oligo concentrations.

## Data
see data folder
## Running it
first model does not account for annealing temperature, but includes pseudoprimers, solve-by-hand cases, and checks CDC primers
second model does attempt to account for annealing temperature but still needs some work
**first website applies our primer specificity model in reverse: it finds possible primers for a given genome and target gene while accounting for specificity, mismatch allowance, GC content, 3' distance of mismatches, mismatch severity, etc.
Limitation: it does not yet include annealing temperature, but the website's first version was tested against reverse-engineered test cases, CDC primers, and we generated some possible cases to see how the primers our website produces compares with NCBI BLAST **
.

# Publishes the two websites on GitHub Pages on every push to main.
# One-time setup: repository Settings -> Pages -> Source: "GitHub Actions".
name: Publish website

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build _site
        run: python3 .github/build_pages.py
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: _site
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

The public website is fine, but there's one privacy issue to deal with. All 10 session logs in `journal/` contain your CMU email address. It's part of the context Claude Code records at the start of each session. Now that the repository is public, anyone can read those files.

They also contain your Mac's folder paths (`/Users/isabelguo/...`), which show your username. That matters much less.

Your options:

1. **Leave it.** A university email is often public anyway, for example in the CMU directory.
2. **Remove it from now on.** I blank the email in the current log files and change the session-log script so future logs leave it out. This is quick and safe, but the email stays visible in older versions of those files in the repository's history.
3. **Remove it completely.** Option 2, plus rewriting the repository's history so no version contains the email, then a force push. That changes every commit ID, so the commit hashes written in your diary and documentation would no longer match. It's hard to undo, so I'd only do it if you say so explicitly.
4. **Make the repository private again.** The website only stays up then if you get the free student plan through GitHub Education, because Pages on a private repository needs a paid plan.

Which would you like? I won't change anything until you choose.

content.text:
Two of the six designs only fully work on Omicron, because they sit on Omicron's spike mutations:
- **Version 2 design 1 is Omicron-only.** Its forward primer and probe cover the spot where Omicron has a 9-base insertion in spike (it adds three amino acids, "EPE", at position 214). The reference, Beta and Delta don't have it, so there's no product on them. That makes it an Omicron detector rather than a general SARS-CoV-2 test.
- **Version 1 design 1** has a reverse primer with 2 mismatches on the other variants, so binding is weak at the annealing temperature. It sits on Omicron's mutations near amino acids 679–681.
- **The other four designs** match all four genomes perfectly.

Neither designer looks at other variants, because each one only sees the genome it's given. I'm still waiting for Primer-BLAST.

# =============================================================================
# COMPARE: OMICRON SPIKE GENE: website Version 1 vs Version 2 vs Primer-BLAST
# =============================================================================
# Target: the spike (S) gene of Omicron BA.1 (data/variants/OL672836.1),
# genome positions 21497-25309 (3,813 bases; found by matching the first and
# last 30 bases of the reference spike, NC_045512.2 21563-25384; Omicron's
# spike deletions and its 9-base insertion make it 9 bases shorter).
#
# Designers, all with the websites' default settings (mismatch allowance 2,
# products 60-150 bp):
#   Version 1   design_primers(annealing_c=None): GC content only
#   Version 2   design_primers(annealing_c=55): temperature + primer dimers
#   NCBI        Primer-BLAST (Primer3 + BLAST), our length/GC/product
#               settings, its own Tm defaults, specificity vs the human
#               genome. Saved in data/ncbi_blast/primer_blast_omicron_spike.txt
#
# For every design:
#   - Tms at qPCR conditions and Version 2's rules (assay_temperature_check)
#   - the assay status at 55 C on the reference, Beta, Delta and Omicron
#     genomes (run_temperature_model: first model + Tm at each site)
#   - for NCBI's designs, where our two versions rank the same product
#
# Run it with:  python3 journal/compare_omicron_spike.py
# =============================================================================

import glob
import os

from compare_ncbi_blast import primer_blast_designs
from first_model_factor_specificity import read_fasta
from primer_design import design_primers, find_target, possible_designs
from second_model_annealing_temp import QPCR_CONDITIONS, assay_temperature_check, run_temperature_model

PROJECT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SPIKE = (21497, 25309)   # 1-based, inclusive, in OL672836.1


def genomes():
    found = {"Wuhan ref": read_fasta(glob.glob(os.path.join(PROJECT, "data", "reference", "*"))[0])[1]}
    for path in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(PROJECT, "data", "variants", "*"))):
        found[os.path.basename(path).split("_")[0]] = read_fasta(path)[1]
    return found


def report(label, forward, reverse, probe, start, end, omicron, all_genomes, extra=""):
    check = assay_temperature_check(forward, reverse, probe, omicron[start - 1:end],
                                    conditions=QPCR_CONDITIONS)
    tms = "/".join(f"{check[k]['tm']:.1f}" for k in ("forward", "reverse", "probe"))
    rules = "pass" if check["ok"] else "; ".join(p.split(":")[0].split(" (")[0] for p in check["problems"])
    status = ", ".join(f"{name} {run_temperature_model(forward, reverse, g, probe=probe, max_mismatches=2)['assay_at_ta']}"
                       for name, g in all_genomes.items())
    print(f"  {label}  {start}-{end} ({end - start + 1} bp){extra}")
    print(f"      F {forward}  R {reverse}  P {probe}")
    print(f"      qPCR Tm F/R/P {tms} C; Version 2 rules: {rules}")
    print(f"      at 55 C: {status}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    all_genomes = genomes()
    omicron = all_genomes["Omicron"]
    spike = omicron[SPIKE[0] - 1:SPIKE[1]]
    assert spike.startswith("ATG") and spike.endswith("TAA") and len(spike) % 3 == 0
    start, end, _ = find_target(omicron, spike)

    for title, annealing in (("VERSION 1 (GC only)", None), ("VERSION 2 (temperature)", 55.0)):
        result = design_primers(omicron, spike, 2, 60, 150, annealing_c=annealing)
        print(f"\n{title}: {result['possible']} possible designs")
        for n, d in enumerate(result["designs"], 1):
            report(f"design {n}", d["forward"]["seq"], d["reverse"]["seq"], d["probe"]["seq"],
                   d["product_start"] + 1, d["product_end"], omicron, all_genomes)

    ranked = {label: {(d["product_start"], d["product_end"]): i + 1
                      for i, d in reversed(list(enumerate(possible_designs(omicron, start, end,
                                                                           annealing_c=ta))))}
              for label, ta in (("v1", None), ("v2", 55.0))}
    print("\nNCBI PRIMER-BLAST")
    path = os.path.join(PROJECT, "data", "ncbi_blast", "primer_blast_omicron_spike.txt")
    for n, d in enumerate(primer_blast_designs(path), 1):
        f, r, p = d["forward"], d["reverse"], d["probe"]
        product = (start + f[1] - 1, start + r[1])
        ranks = ", ".join(f"{label} rank {ranked[label].get(product, '-')}" for label in ("v1", "v2"))
        report(f"design {n}", f[0], r[0], p[0], product[0] + 1, product[1], omicron, all_genomes,
               f"; in our lists: {ranks}")

Primer-BLAST far more than Version 1 does. But neither our designer nor
Primer-BLAST looks at OTHER variants: a design made on one genome can sit on

content.text:
I designed primers for the Omicron spike gene with both website versions and with NCBI Primer-BLAST. None of the three gave the same design as another, but Version 2 is much closer to NCBI than Version 1.

The target was the Omicron BA.1 spike gene, genome positions 21,497–25,309 (3,813 bases, 37 % GC). All three used the websites' default settings. I tested every design on the reference genome, Beta, Delta and Omicron at 55 °C.

**Version 1 (GC content only):**
- **Temperature:** all 3 designs fail Version 2's rules. Primers melt too low (57–60 °C), one pair is 7.2 °C apart, and every probe melts below its primers instead of above.
- **Dimers:** design 1's reverse primer forms a 3′-end dimer that could be extended.
- **Variants:** design 1 sits on an Omicron mutation (N679K), so it binds only weakly on the other three genomes.

**Version 2 (with temperature):**
- **Temperature:** all 3 designs pass, with primers at 63.0–63.3 °C and probes at about 70 °C.
- **Variants:** design 1 is Omicron-only. Its forward primer and probe cover the spot where Omicron has a 9-base insertion in spike ("EPE", position 214), so it gives no product on the other genomes. That's useful for detecting Omicron, but not as a general COVID test.
- **The other two** work on all four genomes.

**NCBI Primer-BLAST:**
- **Variants:** all 10 designs work on all four genomes, and none bind the human genome.
- **Overlap with ours:** none is identical to any of our designs. Four sit in the same stretch as design 3 from both of our versions (24,636–24,730), and three more overlap other designs of ours.
- **Probes:** 6 of the 10 fail one rule. Their probes melt only 0.5–1.9 °C above the primers instead of at least 2 °C, the same weakness Primer-BLAST showed on the N gene.
- **Ranking:** 8 of NCBI's 10 designs rank much higher in Version 2's list than in Version 1's. For example, NCBI design 5 is 187th in Version 2 but 9,507th in Version 1, because Version 2 ranks by Tm the way Primer3 does. NCBI's products are longer (69–150 bp), while both our versions prefer short ones.

**What it shows:** with temperature added, our designer agrees with Primer-BLAST much more closely. But neither our designer nor Primer-BLAST checks other variants, so a design made on one genome can land on that variant's own mutations. Checking each design against several variant genomes would be a good next feature.

**Files (not committed yet; that happens at "bye"):**
- `journal/compare_omicron_spike.py` reruns the whole comparison.
- `data/ncbi_blast/primer_blast_omicron_spike.txt` holds NCBI's raw result.
- `journal/test_cases_web_specificity.txt` has a new part D with the full table and notes.
